zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-checks use Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0, https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html . The scan remains the authority for this transcription.

runs.text: Veſtido feito todo de borra tirando as

lines.note: Watako is a garment made of silk floss or waste silk; the Portuguese excludes its borders, continued below. The damaged d of Veſtido and the word boundary before tirando are restored from the scan.
The edges and bindings are the exceptions to the garment's floss construction. This is the continuation of tirando as, not a separate definition.
Watakushi is the first-person expression glossed Eu. Uye, watakushi contrasts a superior with his dependants or with the speaker, as the next row explains.
Completes Senhor: lord and servants, or lord and I. The final Va- begins the following Japanese example; the printed division is retained.
Watakushina koto wo yuu means stating private or personal opinions. The divided opening completes Va- above, and the Portuguese adjective continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: as, ou de ſua opinião que não tem autoridade,

lines.note: The private opinions lack authority, according to the Portuguese explanation. The scan supports autoridade rather than OCR autoricade; no modern wording is substituted.
The opinions also have no public weight. The printed form pubrico is retained with r rather than silently modernized to publico; OCR puhrico misread the b.
Watagami and watanome name fibres of floss protruding from a garment. The l is the alternative-form marker, while the relative clause continues below.
The fibres emerge through the garment. The example repeats watagami and begins its alternative watanome across the row boundary.

runs.text: Sairem os fios da borra po-

lines.note: Watanome ga deta describes the floss fibres appearing outside the cloth. The visible borra corrects OCR boira; the source's separation tano mega is retained.
Completes pollo: the fibres emerge through thin or open-textured clothing. The tightly set veſtidoralo is preserved rather than imposing a modern word gap.
This distinct watagami denotes armour for the shoulders. It is a separate homograph, not another description of the garment's projecting fibres.

runs.text: Penugem de paßaro, que eſtà no ninho.

lines.note: Watage is the down of a bird still in the nest. Enlargement shows the damaged double-s ligature in paßaro, matching the clearer repeated word on the next row.

runs.text: ¶ Item, O meſmo paßaro cõ penugem.

lines.note: The same word can denote the down-covered young bird itself. The nasal abbreviation cõ remains unexpanded.

runs.text: He o falcão, que eſtà ainda

lines.note: Norige is specified as a falcon still possessing down. The Portuguese qualification continues on the next row, distinguishing this bird-specific use.
The phrase completes the description of the young falcon as still in down. Its short length does not change its status as a separate physical line.

runs.text: Molho de palha brãda com ſal, que

lines.note: Watagomi is a bundle of soft straw mixed with salt, used for preserving a gutted animal. The scan and repeated gomiuo below support gomi, also corroborated by the supplied NINJAL headword index; brãda is nasal-abbreviated branda.

runs.text: metem na barriga dalgũa aue, ou peixe depois

lines.note: The straw is placed inside a bird or fish. The visible peixe corrects OCR prixe; depois introduces the prior removal of the entrails below.

runs.text: de lhe tirar em as tripas pera o fazer duras mui-

lines.note: The entrails are removed so that the animal will keep for a long time. The print appears to give duras, although the intended infinitive is durar; this anomaly and the supplied tirar em spacing are retained.

runs.text: to tempo, porque ſe não corrompa. Vt,

lines.note: Completes muito tempo and explains the preservation purpose: preventing decomposition. Vt introduces the verb phrase divided at Vata-.
Completes watagomi wo suru, to carry out the straw-and-salt preservation procedure. It belongs to the preceding definition rather than beginning a separate gomi entry.

Wataito names a thread made of floss. The weak second letter in berra is retained as the aligned OCR reading, although borra is expected from the surrounding entries; the next clause adds another occasional sense.

runs.text: Seda branda, ou cozida: poſto que mais corrẽ-

lines.note: The occasional sense is soft or boiled silk. The explanation then contrasts this with the more usual terminology, continuing corrente across the row boundary.

Completes corrente and supplies the more usual terms Tçuqeito and Neriguri for the softened silk. The faint e after q and the following i replace the malformed OCR Tçuqrito; the visible forms are preserved without modernization.
Watamashi denotes moving into a new house. The example repeats that noun across the physical division Va-/tamaxi below.
Watamashi wo suru is to make that move. The Portuguese explicitly links eſta mudança to the preceding house-changing definition.

runs.text: Fios da borra que ſam fora do

lines.note: Watanome again names floss fibres showing outside clothing. This standalone entry supplies the alternative previously given under watagami.
Veſtido completes fora do veſtido, specifying that the loose fibres are outside the garment. It remains a distinct physical continuation row.

runs.text: Paſſar de hũa parte a outra,

lines.note: Watari, wataru, watatta denotes crossing from one side to another. The principal parts and doubled long s in the Portuguese Paſſar are visible; the places crossed follow below.
Bridges and rivers exemplify the crossing. Hashi wo wataru gives the bridge example, with its Portuguese equivalent on the following line.
The bridge example is translated first; takoku ye wataru then means going across to another country. The final Paſ- belongs to its Portuguese translation below.
Completes the foreign-country gloss. Umi or ye, sea or inlet, supplies the object of the next wataru example, divided at vata-.
Completes wataru, here sailing across the sea or an inlet. The gloss confirms the two alternative objects in the preceding Japanese example.
The noun watari denotes a passage or crossing. Watari wo suru illustrates making the crossing, distinct from the preceding verb's principal parts.
Watariai denotes meeting while passing, with a more specific hostile sense explained below. The scan restores t in Encontrarenſe; the abbreviation q̃ and long-o carons are retained.

runs.text: são: mas mais propriamente ſe diz dos inimi-

lines.note: Completes paſsão and narrows the meaning to enemies. The visible round s and divided inimi- replace the OCR's cão and inimut-; the mixed s forms across paſ-/são are retained.

runs.text: gos que ſe encontrão, & ferem hus aos outros.

lines.note: Enemies encounter and strike one another. The printed hus is retained without adding a nasal mark merely because hũs would be expected.
Teki ni watariyoo illustrates engaging an enemy. The contracted long-vowel form matches the principal parts of watariai, with the printed caron retained.
Watariawase carries the same encounter or combat sense as watariai. Idem refers back to that entry, while ſuru and eta give the supplied principal parts.
Wataridate is described as a light, easily handled shield. The relative clause continues into its historical use against arrows below.

runs.text: vſauão os Iapões contra as frechas.

lines.note: The shield was used by the Japanese against arrows. Iapões, with its visible nasal mark and e, replaces the OCR's malformed Iapies.

runs.text: Hũs paßadiços, que ha fora dos pa-

lines.note: Varidono denotes covered passages outside a palace or shrine. The print omits the ta of expected wataridono; the supplied NINJAL index independently flags this as a misprint, so the visible headword is preserved.

runs.text: ços do Dairi, ou das ermidas dos Camis.

lines.note: Completes paços and locates the passages outside the imperial palace or the shrines of the kami. Dairi and Camis are Japanese cultural terms embedded in the Portuguese sentence.
Watashi or watashigane names a metal implement. The following description explains its use in the equipment for blackening teeth.

runs.text: metal bem laurado, & polido de que vſão as

lines.note: The implement is carefully worked and polished metal. The relative clause identifies its users on the next physical row.

runs.text: molheres atraueſado ſobre hũa ſelha, ſobre que

lines.note: Women use the implement laid across a tub, supporting the objects described next. The abraded atraueſado and ſobre are restored from their visible strokes and the surrounding construction.

runs.text: poem algũs petrechos com que fazem os den-

lines.note: They set utensils on the support for the tooth-blackening procedure. The open c in petrechos replaces OCR l; the final den- continues dentes below.
Completes dentes pretos, the blackened teeth. The initial t and continuation indentation are restored; the line belongs to the watashigane definition.
Watashi, watasu, wataita means handing over, and then causing something to pass across. The supplied aita preserves the historical s-verb past formation rather than modernizing it to ashita.

runs.text: ſar algũa couſa, ou fazer paßar. Vt,

lines.note: Completes Paſſar and introduces the boat example. The example's object fune is divided from its following particle by the printed row boundary.
Fune wo watasu is to convey the vessel across. The next example begins with Fa-, completed as hashi on the following line.
Hashi wo watasu means building or laying a bridge across something. The Portuguese locates it in the river on the next row.
The river completes the bridge gloss. The next Japanese example describes binding offenders and taking them through the public streets; its main verb follows below.
Watasu completes the public-exposure example. The Portuguese begins the explanation that the offenders are tied and paraded, continuing paſſão below.

runs.text: ſão pollas ruas publicas à vergonha. ¶

lines.note: The bound offenders are taken through public streets in shame. The final Co- starts kotoba in a new example about leaving spoken instructions.
Kotoba wo watasu and iiwatasu are alternative expressions for leaving a verbal message or injunction. The source's compact iyvataſu spelling is preserved.
This completes the explanation of the spoken injunction: to entrust or recommend something verbally. Palaura is retained in its historical spelling.
Watashiawase means encountering or striking one another. The Portuguese alternative ferir is divided across this and the following row.
Completes ferir hum a outro, to strike one another. The reciprocal object belongs to the preceding encounter entry.
Watashibune is a ferryboat. The damaged t is recovered from the scan and the watashi family; OCR Varaxibune would misidentify the word.
Watashigane refers back to watashi, the metal support described in the other column. Vide is the italic cross-reference instruction; its Japanese target remains roman.
Watashimori is the ferryman operating the crossing. The printed-looking Bar queiro separation is retained instead of silently joining the Portuguese noun.
Watazukin is a cap made with floss or padded silk material. The definition places it among the wata textile terms without adding an unprinted material specification.

runs.text: Vatô. Cataru caxira. i, Ienxǔno coſocu.

lines.note: Watoo, literally the head or topic of speech, is explained as the old cases of the Zen school. The printed circumflex in Vatô and caron in Ienxǔ are kept distinct.
The Portuguese describes these as subjects of meditation among the Zen adherents. Ienxùs is embedded in that explanation, with its printed grave accent rather than the preceding headword's caron.
Watteiri means forcing or pushing one's way in. The scan shows two t types in the headword; the following row names the people or vegetation through which one passes.
The action is pushing through a crowd, undergrowth, and similar obstacles. This completes the objects governed by romper in the preceding row.

runs.text: Voz do que chora, ou grita. Vt,

lines.note: Watto represents a cry or shout. The example repeats the exclamation at the line break before its verbs of weeping and crying out.
Watto naki sakebu means crying and shouting aloud. The visible i in gritos corrects OCR grutos, while the Japanese example remains in its historical spelling.
Wawari denotes speaking or shouting in complaint. The Portuguese aqueixando-se is divided across this line and the next.
The complaint is made with vexation or irritation. The final B is the low-register label; enlargement supports retaining its locally sloping type with the italic run.
Wase means to come, with its social usage restricted by the following explanation. The nasal abbreviation gẽ- starts gente across the physical boundary.
Completes gente and specifies ordinary or lower-ranking people as the referents of wase. The historical social distinction is the dictionary's usage explanation.
This homographic wase means early-ripening rice, explained as hayai ine. The visible terminal mark divides the repeated Va-/xe example and replaces OCR Va.
Wase and okute contrast early and late rice. The historical Portuguese ſorodeo is retained rather than replaced with a modern spelling.
Washi is the eagle. The brief Portuguese Aguia supplies the complete definition on this single line.
Washiri is equated with hashiru, to run. The source records the w-initial variant and its principal parts; they are not normalized to the better-known h-initial form.
Wayaku denotes Japanese medicine or a medicinal preparation. The historical Mezinha is the noun for a remedy, not a diminutive to be regularized.

runs.text: Homem mao, ou de ruins manhas.

lines.note: Wayakujin denotes a bad person or one of disreputable habits. The moral characterization comes directly from the Portuguese gloss.
Wayakumono and wayakuna mono carry the same bad-person sense. Idem points to the immediately preceding definition rather than the medicine entry.
Wayakuna kuni is a country of bad people. The example extends the preceding adjectival form from a person to a country.
Wayawayato describes noisy commotion. The Portuguese adverbial explanation begins traquinada, continued on the next physical line.
Completes traquinada and gives the alternative of sounding with a din. Both expressions explain the noisy manner denoted by wayawayato.
Waye is equated with kegare, impurity or dirt. The repeated compound visibly begins Yaye- rather than Vaye-; this printed initial discrepancy is preserved, not silently harmonized.
Completes the compound printed Yaye-fujǒ, referring to impurity. Idem maintains the same dirt or defilement sense; the caron over o is visible.
Wayo is glossed by ichimi and by uniting or making peace. The Portuguese appears to print fzerenſe without the expected a; the anomalous source spelling is retained.
Friendship and peace complete the gloss. Wayo ni naru means becoming reconciled; the faint i has surviving upper and lower strokes, replacing the OCR punctuation after Vayon.
Waza means a work, deed, or action, here rendered simply Obra. The whole entry occupies this single physical row.
Wazan is paraphrased as gently or indirectly accusing, with the Portuguese Accuſação. The scan has no secure punctuation between the Japanese paraphrase and the italic gloss, so none is supplied.
Wazanna mono denotes a person who goes about accusing others. The visible Peßa lacks the expected o of peßoa; its printed form is retained while accu- continues below.

runs.text: ſando os outros, ou dizem o mal delles por di

lines.note: Completes accusando and adds speaking ill of others in various places. The printed dizem is retained despite the singular antecedent, and no terminal hyphen is supplied after di.

runs.text: uerſas partes, ou peßoa e ruim condição, ou

lines.note: Completes diversas partes, then describes a person of bad disposition. The paper split crosses the expected d of de, leaving e visibly; the damaged reading e ruim is retained rather than silently restoring that letter.
Maos bofes, literally bad lungs or temperament, continues the description of an ill-natured person. It closes the wazan example rather than modifying the next adverb.

Wazato means deliberately or on purpose. The damaged gloss visibly begins D, with no secure surviving e of expected De; propoſito restores the faint i omitted by OCR. The paper split is retained as a nonblocking caveat.
Wazawai denotes misfortunes and troubles. The scan supports u in the headword and Males without OCR's extra d; the damaged conjunction retains enough of its ampersand shape to read &.

zones.label: Printed gathering signature
zones.note: A small ink remnant lies to the right of Y where a paper split crosses the signature area; no additional character can be established.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: Anticipates Vazauaza at the opening of the next page (bnf-f0530).
